question: Can training each dense layer through a small unconstrained three-factor mode decomposition reduce parameters and computation while exposing a stable, hierarchical, and interpretable set of latent modes?

key_findings.claim: Mode decomposition learning parameterizes each layer as a rank-at-most-p product and optimizes its two pattern matrices and diagonal importance vector directly.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 1 writes W^l = hat-xi^l Sigma^l (xi^{l+1})^T, with unconstrained, generally nonorthogonal factors and real diagonal scores. Equation 3 and Supplemental Equations S1-S5 give factor-wise gradient updates. The 1L2P variant uses separate incoming and outgoing pattern matrices at a hidden layer, while 1L1P ties the shared hidden-layer pattern across its adjacent weights.

key_findings.claim: On one small MNIST multilayer perceptron, p=30 matches the reported full-weight test accuracy with about 40% as many trainable scalar parameters.
key_findings.evidence: For architecture 784-100-100-10, the full matrices contain 89,400 weights, while the paper counts 35,910 parameters for 1L2P with p=30. Figure 2 reports similar test accuracy over five runs; the supplement also compares SVD training, an identity-middle-factor low-rank parameterization, and spectral learning on the same architecture. This is credible evidence of parameter reduction on this configuration, not evidence of a general compute or scaling law.

anchors.section: Comparison to matrix factorization methods and Figures S2-S3

key_findings.claim: The paper's claim of O(pN) training cost is not established by its experiments or implementation; the demonstrated saving is chiefly parameter count.
key_findings.evidence: The text equates the smaller factor parameterization with training cost, but reports no runtime, FLOPs, memory, hardware, throughput, or energy measurement. The released MDL code repeatedly materializes each dense W as xi1 @ diag(Sigma) @ xi2 and then performs dense forward and backward matrix products. That implementation therefore retains dense-layer work and adds factor reconstruction, rather than executing the factorized O(pN) path. An O(p(N_l+N_{l+1})) layer evaluation is possible algebraically, but it is neither implemented nor benchmarked here.

key_findings.claim: Individual modes and their importance ranking are not identifiable from the learned weight matrix, so the proposed interpretation is gauge-dependent.
key_findings.evidence: The supplement acknowledges that the pattern and importance matrices are not unique. Per-mode rescalings of either pattern can be absorbed into Sigma without changing W, and more general changes of basis preserve a two-factor low-rank product. The proposed tau score depends separately on factor norms and |Sigma|, so it can change under equivalent parameterizations. Equal L2 penalties and robustness to three penalty strengths select an optimization convention but do not make the learned modes intrinsic or unique.

anchors.section: Model, normalization ambiguity and L2 regularization
Mode ranking and definition of tau
Figure S8, factor norms across regularization strengths

key_findings.claim: The claimed advantage over ordinary low-rank decomposition cannot be an expressivity advantage because the two parameterizations define exactly the same rank-p matrix class.
key_findings.evidence: The paper's MDL layer W = hat-xi Sigma xi^T can always be rewritten as (hat-xi Sigma)xi^T, which is the supplement's low-rank decomposition W = AB^T with Sigma fixed to identity; conversely, identity Sigma is a special MDL setting. Figure S2's accuracy gap must therefore arise from optimization, initialization, or regularization, not additional feature-extraction flexibility. The paper reports one learning curve but does not isolate these parameterization effects.

anchors.section: Supplemental Equation S9 and Figure S2

key_findings.claim: The written backpropagation derivation contains an incorrect softmax-cross-entropy gradient and dimensionally swapped factor indices.
key_findings.evidence: For softmax logits with one-hot cross entropy, dC/dz_j is h_j-hat-h_j, not -hat-h_j(1-h_j) as written in the main text and supplement. The displayed recursion for K_i^l uses xi^{l+1}_{i alpha} and hat-xi^l_{j alpha}; i indexes the upstream layer and j the downstream layer, so these factors are reversed relative to Equation 1 and may not even have the stated dimensions. The correct product is hat-xi^l_{i alpha} xi^{l+1}_{j alpha}. The released code uses output-target and dense W^T for error propagation, which limits this finding to the paper's formulas rather than proving that the plotted runs used those erroneous expressions.

key_findings.claim: The reported logarithmic and eventually constant mode-count law is an exploratory MNIST threshold plot, not a demonstrated asymptotic law of deep learning.
key_findings.evidence: The least p is defined as the smallest tested mode count that reaches the BP performance, but no equivalence tolerance, statistical decision rule, search resolution, confidence interval, or held-out architecture is specified. Figures 2(c) and S5 vary only the width of a 784-N-N-10 MNIST MLP, over a finite range in which accuracy visibly saturates. Five runs and two regularization values support a local empirical pattern, but cannot establish lim p/N=0, universality across tasks, or eventual constancy.

anchors.section: Figure S5 and definition of least p

key_findings.claim: The hierarchical geometry and leading-mode evidence is suggestive but confined to post hoc diagnostics whose interpretation depends on the chosen factorization.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 2(d-f) report decreasing pattern-cloud dispersion and lower class-response subspace overlap with depth; Figure 3 reports that removing low-tau modes is less damaging than random removal and fits two slopes around a fixed rank-10 breakpoint. Supplemental Figures S4-S8 repeat the ranking across score choices, widths, and regularization strengths. These are qualitative measurements on MNIST MLPs, without predictive intervention beyond pruning, alternative disentanglement metrics, uncertainty on slopes or breakpoints, or an invariant definition of a mode.

key_findings.claim: The mean-field ODEs accurately track a restricted teacher-student simulation, but they are not a theory of the full deep MNIST training method.
key_findings.evidence: The analytic setting assumes i.i.d. Gaussian inputs, erf activation, one hidden layer, equal teacher and student hidden widths and mode counts, fixed teacher parameters, equal output weights, and learns only the upstream student factor while setting the other factors to their teacher values. Equations S11-S25 close dynamics through Q, M, and P as d tends to infinity. Figure 4 shows close finite-d simulation curves, but gives no quantitative residual or error bars and does not connect those restricted ODEs to multilayer ReLU classification where all factors are trained.

key_findings.claim: The public repository is useful as partial source disclosure but cannot reproduce the published figures in its current state.
key_findings.evidence: The repository provides Python scripts for Figures 1, 2, and 4 plus a Figure 3 notebook, but only names Python 3.8 and omits dependency versions, environment lock, license, seeds for most runs, MNIST files, raw results, and checkpoints. The README says Figure 3 uses presaved models, yet no model or data artifacts are present; the notebook contains placeholder variable 'model', a recorded ValueError, hard-coded rank-10 fits, and a random-pruning branch whose assignment is commented out. Two comparison scripts refer to undefined train/test globals, and the released Figure 4 main block covers only repeated d=30, alpha=1 runs rather than both published panels. Syntax compilation succeeds, but end-to-end reproduction does not.

method.core_idea: Replace every dense weight matrix by trainable low-rank factors, regard their columns as latent modes, and study the learned factor geometry and importance spectrum across depth.
method.mechanism: Each layer uses an upstream factor, a diagonal score vector, and a downstream factor. Gradients are taken with respect to those factors, with either separate incoming/outgoing patterns per hidden layer or a tied hidden pattern shared across adjacent layers. Experiments train ReLU MLPs on MNIST and compare accuracy, parameter counts, factor geometry, mode pruning, and low-rank baselines. A separate erf teacher-student model closes online-learning dynamics through local-field covariance order parameters and integrates their mean-field ODEs.
assumptions: Each weight matrix can be restricted to rank at most p without materially reducing task accuracy.
The trainable factors are unconstrained and receive identical L2 regularization; this does not remove their fundamental nonidentifiability.
The MNIST experiments use fully connected ReLU networks, softmax outputs, Adam-style optimization, fixed mode counts within layers, and architecture-specific learning rates.
The claimed compute scaling assumes factorized contractions are used instead of materializing dense weights, although the released implementation materializes them.
The width law assumes the smallest tested p matching a BP accuracy is a meaningful and stable statistic, despite no stated matching tolerance or asymptotic theory.

The online theory assumes i.i.d. standard Gaussian inputs, erf units, a one-hidden-layer teacher and student with matched sizes and mode counts, thermodynamic input dimension, and only one learned student factor.
The hierarchy interpretation assumes individual factor columns are scientifically meaningful even though equivalent matrix factorizations can change them.

techniques.role: Represents a dense layer by two unconstrained pattern matrices and a diagonal score vector.
Applies minibatch gradient optimization directly to the low-rank factors.
Shares one hidden-layer pattern between incoming and outgoing matrices in the 1L1P variant.
Ranks factor columns by a combined norm-and-score statistic and removes modes to test their functional importance.
Uses principal angles between class-conditioned activation subspaces as a disentanglement diagnostic.
Searches for the smallest mode count reaching a full-weight baseline across hidden widths.
Reduces restricted online teacher-student learning to ODEs for covariance order parameters.

evaluations.setting: MNIST classification with a 784-100-100-10 fully connected network.
evaluations.metric: Test accuracy trajectories, final accuracy versus p, and trainable parameter count over five runs.
evaluations.result: At p=30, 1L2P reportedly matches full-weight training at roughly 98% accuracy using 35,910 versus 89,400 scalar parameters; 1L1P further reduces factors without a visible accuracy loss.
evaluations.baseline: Full-weight backpropagation, with supplemental SVD-training, two-factor low-rank, and spectral-training comparisons.

evaluations.setting: MNIST MLPs with hidden width varied up to about 2,000.
evaluations.metric: Smallest tested p reaching the corresponding full-weight accuracy.
evaluations.result: The plotted threshold grows in two approximately linear regions against log width and appears to saturate, based on five-run experiments and two L2 strengths.
evaluations.baseline: The full-weight accuracy of each same-width architecture.

evaluations.setting: Four- to seven-layer MNIST MLPs trained with p=30 or p=70.
evaluations.metric: Pattern-cloud dispersion, cosine of the first principal angle between class-response subspaces, rank-ordered tau, and accuracy after mode removal.
evaluations.result: Factors appear more compact with depth, class subspaces generally overlap less, and low-ranked modes can be removed with less damage than high-ranked ones; a two-slope rank plot is reported around rank 10.
evaluations.baseline: Full-weight activation subspaces and random mode removal.

evaluations.setting: One-hidden-layer online erf teacher-student regression with Gaussian inputs.
evaluations.metric: Mean-squared error over scaled sample time and qualitative evolution of the teacher-student overlap matrix.
evaluations.result: Mean-field ODE curves visually agree closely with markers for selected finite dimensions and mode loads, and larger mode load shortens plateaus.
evaluations.baseline: Direct one-pass stochastic-gradient simulations of the same restricted synthetic model.

evaluations.metric: Availability of source, dependencies, data, checkpoints, seeds, runnable figure paths, and actual efficiency measurements.
evaluations.result: Partial Python source is public and syntax-valid, but missing data/checkpoints and multiple broken or incomplete paths prevent end-to-end reproduction; no runtime or memory benchmark substantiates compute savings.
evaluations.baseline: A self-contained environment and one-command regeneration of all reported panels.

limitations: The experiments establish parameter reduction only for small fully connected MNIST models; convolutional networks, transformers, modern datasets, and genuinely large-scale training are not evaluated.
The O(pN) cost statement assumes structured factorized execution, but the released implementation reconstructs dense weights and no compute, memory, or wall-clock result is reported.

Factor columns and diagonal scores are non-identifiable under rescaling and change-of-basis symmetries, so individual modes, their geometry, and tau rankings are not intrinsic properties of the learned function.
The three-factor MDL and ordinary two-factor low-rank decomposition have the same rank-p expressivity; their reported accuracy difference is an unseparated optimization or regularization effect.
The paper writes the wrong softmax-cross-entropy logit gradient and swaps upstream/downstream factor indices in its backpropagation recursion.
The least-p scaling plot lacks a matching tolerance, statistical test, search protocol, and broader task replication; finite-width MNIST saturation cannot establish an asymptotic logarithmic law.
The piecewise power law uses a short rank range and a fixed rank-10 breakpoint without model selection, uncertainty on slopes or breakpoint, or comparison to alternative heavy-tailed forms.
The disentanglement measure is only the largest canonical correlation between class-conditioned PCA subspaces, with K varying to explain 80% variance; alternative geometry measures are not tested.
Baseline tuning and compute parity are unclear, and each supplemental factorization comparison is shown on one architecture with method-specific objectives and hyperparameters.
The mean-field analysis freezes two factor families to teacher values and treats a shallow Gaussian erf model, so it does not explain joint factor learning in the deep ReLU classifier.
The public repository has no locked dependencies, dataset, checkpoints, raw numerical results, license, or comprehensive seeds, and its Figure 3 and comparison paths contain executable defects.
The networks omit common architectural components such as biases, convolution, normalization, residual paths, and augmentation, limiting practical conclusions.
failure_modes: Changing an equivalent factor gauge can reorder tau and alter pattern-cloud geometry while leaving every network prediction unchanged.
A small p can create an optimization bottleneck or irreducible rank bottleneck on tasks whose useful representations are not low rank.
Materializing W at every update can make the nominally low-parameter model slower and more memory-intensive than a genuinely factorized implementation.
Accuracy saturation can make many p values look equivalent and create a spurious constant or logarithmic threshold law.
Separate tuning or implicit regularization can make algebraically equivalent two- and three-factor models appear to have different representational power.
The incorrect written output gradient or index recursion will produce wrong implementations if followed literally rather than copied from the repository.
Mode pruning based on a non-invariant score can delete a different functional subspace after harmless factor rescaling or mixing.
A manually chosen breakpoint on a short rank plot can manufacture a convincing piecewise power law.
Mean-field predictions can fail for structured inputs, finite width, ReLU nonlinearities, unequal teacher/student models, or joint learning of all factors.
Missing checkpoints, undefined globals, an inactive random-pruning branch, and absent dataset paths prevent exact regeneration of published plots.
reusable_insights: Separate parameter count, arithmetic complexity, activation memory, optimizer state, and measured wall-clock cost when evaluating factorized training.
Execute low-rank layers as successive thin contractions; rebuilding the dense matrix forfeits the intended computational advantage.
Treat learned factors as coordinates with gauge freedom unless an identifiable convention or invariant observable is supplied.
When two parameterizations describe the same function class, attribute performance gaps to optimization and implicit regularization and design controls to isolate them.
Define low-rank adequacy with a preregistered accuracy tolerance and uncertainty interval before fitting width-scaling laws.
Use change-point selection, held-out widths, and competing distributional fits before calling a ranked spectrum piecewise power-law.
Mode-ablation curves are more informative when the ablated object is an invariant subspace or singular component rather than a non-identifiable factor column.
A mean-field result should state exactly which factors learn and which are teacher-fixed before being used to explain an empirical architecture.
Release the precise environment, immutable data hashes, seeds, checkpoints, raw metrics, and executable figure commands together with a training-efficiency paper.
open_questions: Can an invariant mode definition based on singular subspaces, quotient geometry, or canonical balancing preserve the proposed hierarchy while removing factor gauge dependence?
Does a genuinely factorized kernel deliver end-to-end speed, memory, and energy gains for MDL at matched accuracy on current accelerators?
After matched tuning, do the separate diagonal scores improve optimization over an algebraically equivalent two-factor model, and through what implicit regularizer?
Does the least adequate rank scale logarithmically on CIFAR, ImageNet, language modeling, and structured scientific tasks under a fixed statistical equivalence rule?
Do the rank spectra retain a selected change point and predictive power on held-out runs, or are smoother heavy-tailed models sufficient?
Which factor-geometry conclusions survive gauge balancing, orthogonalization, and alternative disentanglement measures?
Can mean-field dynamics be derived when all three factors learn jointly and then extended from shallow erf teachers to deep ReLU networks?
How do adaptive-rank methods compare with fixed-p MDL in accuracy, stability, runtime, and interpretability?
Can the authors release the exact checkpoints and repair the random-pruning, baseline, and Figure 4 scripts so every panel is independently reproducible?

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Low-rank Deep Neural Networks via Singular Vector Orthogonality Regularization and Singular Value Sparsification
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct prior work training decomposed weights with explicit singular-vector and singular-value structure.
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang et al. enforce an identifiable SVD-like form and induce/prune rank to target deployment computation. MDL removes orthogonality and positivity constraints and emphasizes latent-pattern geometry, but thereby loses mode identifiability and tests efficiency less directly.
competitive_landscape.source_version: Primary arXiv record and CVPRW 2020 status checked 2026-08-24

competitive_landscape.title: Low-rank lottery tickets: finding efficient low-rank neural networks via matrix differential equations
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporaneous direct competitor for low-rank training with adaptive ranks and measured resource reduction.
competitive_landscape.difference: Schotthofer et al. constrain updates to a low-rank manifold, adapt ranks dynamically, provide approximation/stability/descent guarantees, and evaluate time and memory on fully connected and convolutional networks. MDL uses simpler unconstrained fixed-rank factors and adds interpretability claims, but provides neither those guarantees nor actual resource benchmarks.
competitive_landscape.source_version: Primary arXiv v2 and official NeurIPS 2022 records checked 2026-08-24

competitive_landscape.title: ReLoRA: High-Rank Training Through Low-Rank Updates
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later parameter-efficient pretraining method that uses repeated low-rank updates without permanently restricting the final model rank.
competitive_landscape.difference: ReLoRA scales to transformer language models up to 1.3B parameters and reports GPU memory and 9-40% speed improvements. It targets high-rank capacity rather than interpretable fixed modes, but supplies the systems evidence missing from MDL's training-cost claim.
competitive_landscape.source_version: Primary arXiv and official ICLR 2024 records checked 2026-08-24

competitive_landscape.title: Harnessing Orthogonality to Train Low-Rank Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later adaptive low-rank training based on stabilization of orthogonal weight bases.
competitive_landscape.difference: OIALR transitions from full rank, periodically updates identifiable SVD bases and rank, and evaluates ViTs, ImageNet, time series, parameter fraction, accuracy, and training time with public implementations. MDL starts with fixed low rank and studies unconstrained factor modes on MNIST, making it simpler but much less validated and less identifiable.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors present mode decomposition learning as a cheap and interpretable alternative to weight-space training, with logarithmic mode-count scaling, progressively compact and disentangled hierarchical modes, a piecewise power-law importance spectrum, and mean-field specialization dynamics.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper jointly trains unconstrained factor columns, defines 1L2P and tied 1L1P variants, reports parameter-matched MNIST accuracy and factor diagnostics, performs mode-removal experiments, and derives order-parameter ODEs for a restricted online teacher-student model.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Direct low-rank factor training substantially predates this paper, and the extra diagonal factor does not enlarge the two-factor rank-p function class. The distinctive contribution is the physics-motivated attempt to interpret factor columns as a hierarchy and connect them to online specialization. That interpretation remains exploratory because the modes are non-identifiable, the scaling and power-law claims are narrow post hoc observations, the written gradient has errors, and the released artifact cannot reproduce the figures. The robust contribution is a small-model parameterization study and a restricted mean-field calculation, not a demonstrated general law or systems-efficient training framework.
